newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU move on car spare parts sparks industry row.
newsitem.headline: EU move on car spare parts sparks industry row.

text.p: European Union internal trade ministers are set to admit defeat on Thursday in their effort to agree common rules on protecting design in the EU's huge car spare parts market, EU diplomats say.
The issue sets European car manufacturers against the companies which make spare parts for their models.

The ministers are expected to exclude spare parts from a plan to harmonise EU legislation on protecting industrial designs and models. Member states would therefore continue to set their own national rules, the diplomats said.
The move will disappoint the parts industry, which says that thousands of independent spare parts and repair businesses are at risk.

European car manufacturers dispute that argument, saying the present situation would not change. They reject charges that they could monopolise the market for spare parts such as windscreens and door panels.

The ministers are expected to defy the will of the European Commission, which wanted the legislation to include a so-called "repairs clause" allowing independent manufacturers to copy spare parts in exchange for a fee.
EU diplomats say they expect the package to be adopted unanimously on Thursday without the repairs clause.
But the final outcome is still uncertain as it must also be approved by the European Parliament, which may seek negotiations with EU member states.

The debate involves legislation on harmonised EU rules to protect industrial designs from illegal copying if they fulfil certain criteria -- for example, they have to be new and have an individual character.

But accepting suggestions by the European Parliament and arguing that it was a special case, EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti proposed allowing spare parts to be freely copied if parts makers paid a "fair and reasonable" sum to the car manufacturer.
That drew fire from car manufacturers and EU states including France and Germany.
A Dutch official said most member states opposed the "repairs clause" because they saw practical problems.
Marc Greven, legal director at the European car manufacturers' association ACEA, said it would have deprived car makers of full rewards for their investment in research and innovation.

ACEA wanted EU harmonisation of design protection rules, but not according to the Commission's proposal. He noted that Britain was the only EU country now where carmakers could not get design protection for spare parts.
"We want harmonisation more or less on the basis of what exists in most member states today," he said.

However, an industry body representing consumers, insurers, and makers and distributors of spare parts said the ministerial proposal would "give free rein to a 25-year monopoly for EU car makers in the supply of spare car body parts to consumers".
ECAR (European Campaign for the Freedom of the Automotive Parts & Repair Market) warned of the consequences.

"The livelihoods of thousands of independent spare parts and repairs businesses will be threatened and the EU's 180 million vehicle owners who spend more than 30 billion Ecus ($34 billion) each year on car body repairs can expect to face sharply increased costs which will feed through into higher insurance premiums," ECAR spokesman Rupert Hughes said in a statement.
But ACEA's Greven said ECAR was making false claims.
He agreed that the Commission's proposal could increase competition but allow the independents to take a "free ride" on the investments of car manufacturers.
